newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: IATA challenges new British airport noise limits.
newsitem.headline: IATA challenges new British airport noise limits.

text.p: The global airlines body IATA said on Friday it had filed for judicial review of new British limits on aircraft noise at London airports, arguing that many planes "would find themselves simply unable to take off".
Separately, a spokesman for the International Air Transport Association (IATA), which has 253 member carriers, criticised another British decision to double airport taxes for departing passengers.
IATA said it had had no alternative but to mount a legal challenge through the High Court in London against more stringent noise regulations decreed in August by Britain's Department of Transport.

"This is a rare and reluctant step for IATA," the Geneva-based body said in a statement. Airlines worldwide would be affected by the new rules, to apply at London's three airports -- Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted -- from January 1.

Many of the 131 IATA airlines using London's airports "would find themselves simply unable to take off without systematically off-loading large amounts of cargo and large numbers of passengers from many flights, or without introducing an intermediate stop on many of their long-haul destinations," it said in a statement.
"To operate in this way would be completely uneconomic," the statement added. The action was filed late on Thursday.

Under the rule, noise limits for planes departing from the three airports are to be reduced by three decibels to 94 decibels between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m. and by two decibels for night operations from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.
"These proposed noise limits are more severe than at other international gateways. And they were unilaterally introduced," an IATA spokesman said.

Airlines are trying to phase out aircraft with noisier engines to bring their fleets into line with measures laid down by the Montreal-based United Nations' International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO).
Under an ICAO resolution, adopted in 1990 and implemented by Britain, noisier so-called "Chapter Two" aircraft are to be phased out by 31 March 2002.
These aircraft represent roughly one-third of those in operation, and are to be gradually replaced by newly-developed and quieter "Chapter Three" planes.
"The new noise limits would effectively bring forward this phase-out date," the IATA statement said.

"Airlines operating out of London had a legitimate expectation that they would be able to complete their fleet renewal by the ICAO phase-out date, and had built this expectation into their fleet replacement planning," it added.
The new passenger taxes, unrelated to the noise issue, were announced on Tuesday by Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer (economy minister) Kenneth Clarke in his budget speech.
Due to go into effect on November 1 next year, they have already been condemned by the major British airline BA.
The five pound ($8.40) rate on flights to most European countries will be increased to 10 pounds, and an existing 10 pound tax on flights to the rest of the world will be increased to 20.

Asked about the move, a spokesman said IATA was disturbed "because the taxes have nothing to do with civil aviation. The revenues are not being ploughed back into civil aviation, they are simply to fill a hole in the U.K. budget deficit."
He added: "Any money extracted from air transport and passengers should be used to remedy deficiences in airport infrastructure." ($1=.5956 Pound)
